lead: This unit explains what a blockchain is, where it came from, and why it is more than Bitcoin. By the end you can tell a distributed ledger from a distributed database, choose a public, private or consortium chain for a task, and read the header and transactions inside a block.
about: The unit starts with the history in 1.1, from early digital cash to Bitcoin and Ethereum, so later terms have a timeline. Chapter 1.2 compares distributed systems, distributed databases and distributed ledgers, and names the coordination problems that a ledger must solve. Chapter 1.3 explains decentralization and the routes to it, which sets up the features, potential and myths in 1.4. Chapter 1.5 classifies chains by who may join and validate, and 1.6 opens a block to show its header, transactions and hash links. Chapter 1.7 closes with the peer-to-peer network and node roles that keep copies of the chain alive.

chapters.idea: Blockchain grew from digital-cash ideas and Bitcoin's 2008 design into a general shared-ledger technology.
chapters.depth: Cover pre-Bitcoin digital cash, the 2008 Bitcoin whitepaper by Satoshi Nakamoto and the 2009 genesis block; define blockchain separately from Bitcoin; trace growth as currency (blockchain 1.0), smart contracts with Ethereum (2.0), and wider enterprise use (3.0); mention scaling debates and consortium chains as growth signs. Some syllabi call this the growth of blockchain technology. Keep dates to well-known milestones.

figure.title: Growth of blockchain
figure.aria: A timeline from pre-Bitcoin digital cash through the 2008 whitepaper, 2009 genesis block and Bitcoin growth to Ethereum smart contracts and enterprise ledgers.

chapters.example: A student writes: 'Blockchain began in 2015 when Ethereum launched, and Bitcoin is the same thing.' Correct the statement using three dates: 2008, 2009 and 2015. How many years separate the Bitcoin whitepaper from the Ethereum launch? Answer: the whitepaper is 2008, the Bitcoin genesis block is 2009, and Ethereum launched in 2015, so 7 years separate them; blockchain is the shared-ledger idea, Bitcoin is one use of it.
chapters.trap: Calling Bitcoin and blockchain the same, or starting blockchain history at Ethereum.
chapters.prereq: None; this is the opening chapter.
chapters.leave: Cryptographic details to Unit 2, Bitcoin transactions to Unit 4, Ethereum and smart contracts to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A distributed ledger is a replicated, append-only database with shared validation, and it exists because ordinary distributed databases leave trust and conflict handling to an administrator.
chapters.depth: Define distributed system, distributed database (replication, fragmentation, transparency, concurrency, CAP trade-off) and distributed ledger (append-only, replicated, cryptographically linked). Cover limitations of distributed databases: admin trust, conflict resolution, reconciliation, availability versus consistency, query needs. Explain ledgers and double-entry bookkeeping in financial systems. Compare distributed database versus blockchain and DLT versus blockchain. Introduce the Two Generals and Byzantine Generals problems as coordination and fault-tolerance problems; distinguish crash fault from Byzantine fault. Do not teach PoW or BFT algorithms.

figure.title: Four sites, one ledger
figure.aria: Four sites each hold the same three blocks B1, B2 and B3, showing replicated ledger copies with the latest block highlighted.

chapters.example: A bank runs a distributed database with 4 sites. A customer's balance of ₹10,000 is replicated at all 4 sites. Two withdrawals of ₹8,000 each are accepted locally at site 1 and site 2 at the same time, to be reconciled later. Explain why an overdraft can appear, and how a distributed ledger with shared validation avoids it.
chapters.trap: Saying a distributed database is automatically a blockchain; replication is not the same as shared validation and append-only hash-linked blocks.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1 for Bitcoin as an example of a distributed ledger.
chapters.leave: Hash functions and Merkle trees to Unit 2; consensus algorithms to Unit 3; transaction and block formats to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Decentralization moves control from one authority to many participants, and blockchain is one route to it, not the only route.
chapters.depth: Define centralization, decentralization and distribution; give reasons to decentralize (single point of failure, censorship, trust, cost, transparency) and costs (coordination, speed, governance). Cover methods: disintermediation, open participation, replicated data, shared validation, token incentives; partial versus full decentralization; routes from a central service to a decentralized ecosystem: replicate, open read and write, shared consensus, smart contracts, DAO. Introduce decentralized organizations and platforms only as destinations. Some syllabi use other names for the methods; keep the mechanism clear.

figure.title: Routes to decentralization
figure.aria: A route from one writer to many replicas, then shared validation, smart contracts and a DAO.

chapters.example: A firm has 1 head-office server and 6 branch databases. The head office alone can write; branches get read-only copies. Is this centralized, decentralized or distributed? Later all 6 branches validate writes on a shared ledger. Which route did the firm take, and which part is still centralized?
chapters.trap: Saying a system is decentralized because it runs on many machines; decentralization is about who controls writes and validation.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2 for distributed systems and shared ledgers.
chapters.leave: Consensus algorithms to Unit 3; smart contract coding and DAOs to Unit 5; application cases to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Blockchain features are real but conditional, and every claimed benefit has a cost or limit.
chapters.depth: List features: tamper-evidence, transparency, auditability, availability, pseudonymity, programmability, disintermediation; pair each with a limit (51% collusion, privacy, throughput, fees, key loss, oracle trust). Cover potential in payments, records, supply chains, identity and voting only as a map. Bust myths: unhackable, anonymous, always cheaper or faster, trustless, on-chain data always true, smart contract always legal. Some syllabi call this features and potential of blockchain.

figure.aria: Common blockchain claims around a central node, each labelled with a limit such as a 45% pool, public addresses and a fee.

chapters.example: A startup claims its blockchain is unhackable, anonymous and free. Test the three claims with numbers: it has 5 mining pools, the top pool has 45% of hash power; addresses are public; the average fee is ₹40 per transaction. Which claims fail and why?
chapters.trap: Listing features as guaranteed benefits; exam answers should pair each feature with its cost.
chapters.leave: Detailed applications to Unit 6, cryptography to Unit 2, consensus attacks to Unit 3 and Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Blockchains are classified by who may read, write and validate: public, private or consortium.
chapters.depth: Classify by read, write and validate permissions: public permissionless, private permissioned, consortium or federated; add hybrid only as a note. Compare trust, speed, cost, privacy, governance, validator set and examples (Bitcoin public; Hyperledger Fabric private or consortium, but leave details). Explain that permissioned does not mean centralized by default. Some syllabi use public, private and consortium as the three types.

figure.aria: A decision tree: anyone can join a public chain; invited members form a permissioned chain that is private for one organisation or a consortium for many organisations.

chapters.example: A land registry has 1 registrar and 12 sub-registrar offices. Citizens may read records but not write. A trade-finance chain is run by 3 banks. Choose a blockchain type for each case and give one reason based on who validates.
chapters.trap: Calling private chains 'not blockchain' or assuming public is always better; permissioned chains still use blocks and shared validation.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4 on features and Chapter 3 on decentralization.
chapters.leave: Hyperledger Fabric details to Unit 6, consensus choices to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A blockchain is an append-only chain of blocks, each holding a header and transactions, linked by the hash of the previous block.
chapters.depth: Cover architecture layers: application, consensus, network and data. A block is header plus body; header fields: version, previous block hash, Merkle root, timestamp, difficulty or target, nonce; body: transaction list and count. Explain genesis block, block height, hash-pointer linking, candidate block, and why changing a transaction changes the Merkle root, header hash and later blocks. Introduce the Merkle root but leave tree construction to Unit 2. Some syllabi call this overview and structure of a block.

figure.aria: A block tree with a header holding previous hash, Merkle root, time and nonce, and a body holding three transactions.

chapters.example: Block 20 has previous hash 0000a1, Merkle root 7c2e, nonce 18, and 3 transactions. Block 21 is mined with the hash of Block 20 as its previous hash. Tx 2 in Block 20 is edited. Which fields of Block 20 and Block 21 change, and what must happen for the chain to accept the edit?
chapters.trap: Saying the block hash is the hash of the transactions only; it is the hash of the header, which includes the Merkle root.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2 on distributed ledgers and Chapter 5 on chain types.
chapters.leave: Hash functions and Merkle tree construction to Unit 2; transaction scripts to Unit 4; consensus to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A blockchain network is a peer-to-peer network of nodes that validate, relay and store blocks according to their role.
chapters.depth: Define a blockchain network as a P2P overlay. Node roles: full or archive, pruned, mining or validator, light or SPV, wallet, seed; what each stores and validates. Cover transaction and block propagation by gossip, mempool briefly, network size and topology versus decentralization, and test networks. Leave P2P discovery and the full transaction life cycle to Unit 3. Some syllabi call this blockchain networks and nodes.

figure.aria: A peer-to-peer graph with four full nodes, three of them mining, and two light wallets attached to full nodes.

chapters.example: A test network has 4 full nodes; 3 of them also mine. It has 2 light wallets. A light wallet sends 1 transaction. Which nodes relay it, which validate it, which store the full block, and which store only headers? If all 4 full nodes stop, can the 2 light wallets confirm the transaction?
chapters.trap: Assuming every node stores the whole chain and mines; light nodes store headers and rely on full nodes.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6 on blocks and Chapter 2 on distributed systems.
chapters.leave: P2P discovery, transaction life cycle, mining and consensus to Unit 3; wallets to Unit 4.
